phonemes.desc: Welsh; the w is a full vowel (“oo”), so the name is “GRON-oo”.
“The Strong” — pebyr/pebr is the epithet; the compound means Gronw the Strong.
The name survives in the Fourth Branch of the Mabinogi, the Math fab Mathonwy cycle.

pronunciation.approximation: “GRON-oo PEBR” — two words, the second meaning “the strong”

kin.label: Epithet
kin.form: Gronw Pebyr — the fuller spelling of “the strong”

kin.label: Cycle
kin.form: the Fourth Branch of the Mabinogi (Math fab Mathonwy)

pronunciation.note: His story is the Mabinogi’s darkest: the lover who killed Lleu Llaw Gyffes with the only spear that could, cast through a bath-house wall.

domains.title: Gronw the Strong
domains.subtitle: The Spear-Caster of the River Cynfael
domains.lead: Gronw Pebr is the Mabinogi’s tragic villain: the lord of Penllyn who loved Blodeuwedd, the wife fashioned of flowers for Lleu Llaw Gyffes, and who — guided by her — cast the spear that could kill the seemingly invulnerable hero through the bath-house wall. The Fourth Branch’s justice is symmetrical and severe: Lleu’s return, Gronw’s plea, and the stone that still bears the mark of the spear he asked to be placed between himself and the fatal throw.

cards.name: The Spear
cards.desc: He cast the year-wrought, dawn-forged spear through the bath-house wall — the only weapon that could wound Lleu.

cards.name: Blodeuwedd
cards.desc: The flower-wife he loved — her name means “flower-face”; their plot killed her husband.

cards.name: The Bath-House
cards.desc: The one door through which Lleu could be killed: standing with one foot on bath and one on goat-skin, spear through the wall.

cards.name: The Stone
cards.desc: His last plea: a stone between himself and Lleu’s return-cast — the spear went through it, and him.

mythology.lead: Gronw’s mythology is the Fourth Branch’s dark triangle: the man, the flower-wife, and the hero engineered to be unkillable. The Mabinogi tells it without relish and without excuse — the one Welsh narrative in which adultery, murder, and retribution each get exactly their due, and the landscape itself (the Cynfael river, the stone at the bank) keeps the receipt.

myths.title: The Flower-Wife’s Plot
myths.text: Blodeuwedd, made of flowers by Gwydion and Math for the cursed Lleu, met Gronw by the Cynfael and loved him. Her husband’s invulnerability had one precise condition — he could be killed only while standing with one foot on a bath and one on a goat-skin, and only by a spear worked a year at the dark of the moon. She persuaded Lleu to demonstrate the posture; Gronw waited behind the bath-house wall with the finished spear.

myths.title: The Cast Through the Wall
myths.text: The cast went through the wall and through Lleu, who changed into an eagle and vanished into the forest. Gronw took Blodeuwedd and Lleu’s lands. But Lleu was found, healed by Gwydion’s wizardry, and returned in a year’s turning — the cursed hero restored by the uncle whose flower-magic had made the wife who betrayed him.

myths.title: The Stone of the Return-Cast
myths.text: The law of the tale is exact symmetry. Gronw offered compensation — land, gold, any price — and Lleu refused all but one thing: the return-cast. Gronw’s single plea was granted: a stone between him and the spear. The cast went through the stone and through Gronw, and the stone stood by the Cynfael for centuries as the tale’s material proof — the Mabinogi’s most literal monument.

myths.title: The River Cynfael’s Mark
myths.text: Welsh tradition placed the story in the real country of Penllyn and the river Cynfael — the spear-stone was shown to travellers as a landmark, the narrative pinned to the map like a deed. The Mabinogi’s habit of grounding its marvels in named places makes Gronw’s story the Welsh myth-cycle’s most topographically anchored tragedy.

lore.syncretism: Gronw is the Welsh cousin of the Indo-European adulter-killer pattern — the lover who strikes the unkillable hero at his one vulnerable posture — but the Mabinogi’s telling is its own: the magic is legalistic, the justice symmetrical, and the villain allowed his one dignified plea. The flower-wife Blodeuwedd’s fate (changed into an owl, shunned by the other birds) outshines his in later retellings; his stone keeps his share.
lore.culturalLegacy: The Fourth Branch is the most retold of the Mabinogi — Saunders Lewis’s drama Blodeuwedd and a hundred retellings keep the triangle current. The spear-stone tradition fed the Welsh habit of reading the landscape as document; and Gronw’s name, though minor, anchors the Mabinogi’s most exportable story in its most Welsh particulars.
lore.extendedMeditation: Gronw Pebr: the strong one, undone by the one thing strength could not block — the spear he himself had forged for another’s death. Restored plainly, his name keeps the Mabinogi’s lesson in two short words: the stone you ask for may be the only thing the return-cast needs to prove.

sources.name: Math fab Mathonwy (the Fourth Branch of the Mabinogi)
White Book of Rhydderch / Red Book of Hergest manuscripts

lore.archaeology: Gronw leaves the spear-stone of the Cynfael valley — a tradition-landmark, not an excavation. The Mabinogi’s manuscripts (White Book, Red Book) are his monument, as they are for the whole Welsh myth-cycle.
lore.cult: No cult; the Mabinogi’s recitation — the cyfarwyddyd tradition of the storyteller — is his memorial. Modern Welsh revival gatherings stage the Fourth Branch most often of all.
lore.iconography: The spear-caster behind the bath-house wall, or the stone with the hole through it. His icon is the pierced stone — the landmark that outlived the hand that made it necessary.
lore.reception: Celtic studies uses the Fourth Branch as the masterclass of Welsh narrative craft — the legalistic magic, the symmetry of retribution — with Gronw as its necessary third corner. Modern Welsh literature keeps returning to the triangle; and the story’s landscape-pinning is cited wherever myth-and-place is studied.
